newsitem.title: USA: Report says Tibetan rebels trained in United States.
newsitem.headline: Report says Tibetan rebels trained in United States.

text.p: The CIA trained as many as 400 Tibetan exiles at an Army base in Colorado as part of a U.S. government-financed guerrilla war against the mountain kingdon's Chinese rulers beginning in the late 1950s, a newspaper reported on Sunday.

The Chicago Tribune in a detailed report from Nepal which quoted Tibetan sources as well as veterans of the conflict now living in Katmandu said the exiles were also sent to Okinawa and Guam for training in a campaign which the elder brother of the Dalai Lama, Tibet's exiled pacifist leader, helped coordinate.

The guerillas were parachuted back into Tibet where they waged a costly but unsuccessful campaign against the Chinese, who had annexed the country in 1950, the report said. It said the United States ended its involvement in 1968.
"None of us knew how to fight the Chinese the modern way," Nawang Gayltsen, a Katmandu rug merchant trained in Colorado, told the newspaper.
"But the Americans taught us. We learned camouflage, spy photography, guns and radio operation. We played Ping-Pong on Sundays," he said.
The dispatch quoted Tibetan sources as saying that from 200 to 400 exiles were trained at a boot camp inside Camp Hale, a now-abandoned U.S. Army base in Colorado's Rocky Mountains.
Nawang told the newspaper he was flown back to India after training where he helped keep track of guerrilla fighters from an Indian-CIA command post in New Delhi.
"We are old, and we will be gone soon. People should know that men died for this. These things are no longer secrets. They stopped being secrets when we lost," the 63-year-old Nawang said.

The newspaper also quoted a retired CIA agent as saying the object of the guerilla campaign was "to make Tibet very expensive for China ... the guerillas were were supposed to harass them, tie up troops, generally make life miserable. And for a while they actually succeeded."
The report said the Dalai Lama has declined to talk about U.S. involvement in his homeland, and said the CIA through a spokesman said it ws unable to comment on any aspect of the story.
